question: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?
title: Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) — small focused interfaces
direct_answer: The Interface Segregation Principle says clients should not be forced to depend on operations they do not use. Prefer focused contracts shaped around client capabilities instead of one broad interface for every consumer. A class may implement several small interfaces when it genuinely provides several capabilities.

sections.title: Understanding Interface Segregation Principle
sections.content:
The **Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)** is about the client side of a contract. A class should not have to know about methods it never calls, and an implementation should not claim capabilities it cannot provide.

For example, a `Robot` may implement `Workable`, while a `HumanWorker` can implement both `Workable` and `Breakable`. A single `Worker` interface containing `work()`, `eat()`, and `sleep()` would force the robot to expose meaningless operations.

Small does not mean one method by rule. The interface should describe one coherent capability for its clients. Too many tiny interfaces can also make a design hard to navigate, so split where consumers, implementations, or change reasons genuinely differ.

sections.content:
amber|Many Small Interfaces|~ISP core|clients depend only on what they use|no forced unused methods
blue|Fat Interface|~the problem|one big interface|impls stub methods they don't need
emerald|The Fix|~split by role|Printer, Scanner, Fax separate|implement only what fits
violet|Payoff|~loose coupling|change one role → others unaffected

sections.title: Fat Interface vs ISP-Compliant Design
When to Apply ISP
sections.content:
Apply ISP when you are designing interfaces that will have multiple implementations with **different capabilities**. For example, in a payment system, not all payment methods support refunds — credit cards do, but gift cards might not. Instead of one PaymentProcessor interface with a refund method that gift card processors must stub out, split it into PaymentProcessor and RefundablePayment.

Use ISP when you notice implementing classes throwing UnsupportedOperationException or leaving methods empty. In Spring Boot services, if you have a UserService with 15 methods but some controllers only need getUserById, create a **ReadOnlyUserService** interface with just that method.

Apply ISP in plugin architectures where different plugins provide different subsets of functionality.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Splitting by method count**: group operations that clients use as one coherent capability.
- **Using default methods as a substitute for design**: a default can ease compatibility, but clients still see the method.
- **Making one interface per class automatically**: start from consumer needs, not a naming convention.
- **Forgetting the client view**: an implementation may use a larger internal API while exposing a focused application contract.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The Interface Segregation Principle says clients should not be forced to depend on operations they do not use. The interface should be shaped around a coherent capability required by its consumers, rather than becoming a catalogue of everything one implementation can do.

For example, a robot may implement `Workable`, while a human worker implements both `Workable` and `Breakable`. A broad `Worker` interface containing `work`, `eat`, and `sleep` would force the robot to expose methods that have no valid meaning. Focused contracts let each consumer and implementation use only the capability it understands.

ISP does not require one method per interface. The boundary is useful when clients, implementations, or change reasons differ. Too many microscopic interfaces can add noise, so the goal is a small coherent contract, not the smallest possible file.

question: What is a fat interface and why is it a problem?
title: Fat interfaces — what they are and why they violate ISP
direct_answer: A fat interface combines too many unrelated capabilities. Clients depend on methods they never call, and implementations may need meaningless stubs or unsupported operations. Adding an abstract method can also force relevant implementers to change. Split the contract by real client capabilities, while avoiding arbitrary one-method fragmentation.

sections.title: What Makes an Interface Fat
sections.content:
A **fat interface** exposes a wide set of operations to clients that need only a subset. It often mixes concerns such as reading customers, changing them, sending notifications, and producing reports.

The cost appears on both sides. A read-only consumer receives write methods it should not use, while a read-only implementation may be unable to honour them. Adding a new abstract method requires implementers to provide it; a Java default method can reduce source breakage, but it does not fix an incoherent contract.

Split by capability and consumer: `CustomerReader`, `CustomerWriter`, and `CustomerReporter` are useful only if those groups have distinct clients or implementations. The goal is accurate contracts, not a large number of tiny interfaces.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Fat Interface|~too many methods|unrelated capabilities lumped|Machine: print + scan + fax
blue|The Pain|~forced stubs|SimplePrinter throws on scan()|an LSP violation too
emerald|Why It Grows|~convenience|added over time|nobody splits it
violet|The Fix|~segregate|role interfaces|compose where needed

sections.title: Identifying a Fat Interface
When Fat Interfaces Appear
sections.content: Fat interfaces often emerge during **rapid prototyping** when developers keep adding methods to an existing interface instead of refactoring. They appear in **legacy codebases** where an interface has grown over years as new requirements were bolted on. You will see them in **frameworks that try to be everything** — a single interface that handles persistence, validation, caching, and logging. Fat interfaces are common in **CRUD services** that start simple but accumulate business logic, reporting, and notification methods over time. They also appear when teams skip **interface design reviews** and let interfaces grow organically without governance. In Spring Boot apps, a single service interface that handles both commands (write) and queries (read) plus notifications is a red flag for a fat interface.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Judging only by size**: ten cohesive methods used by the same clients can be better than five unrelated ones.
- **Treating every UnsupportedOperationException as proof**: first check whether the operation is guaranteed or documented as optional.
- **Splitting without a client**: a new interface should represent a real capability or usage boundary.
- **Leaving consumers typed to the old fat interface**: the narrower contract must be used at dependency boundaries.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: A fat interface mixes capabilities that its clients do not all need.
It creates accidental dependencies and may force meaningless implementations.
New abstract methods can cause broad implementation changes; default methods do not fix poor cohesion.
Split the contract according to real client capabilities.
Avoid replacing one fat interface with arbitrary one-method clutter.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A fat interface is a contract that combines too many unrelated capabilities. A reporting component may need only customer reads but still depend on methods for deletion, notification, and export. A read-only implementation may then need empty methods or runtime exceptions for operations it cannot support.

For example, `CustomerService` can be separated into `CustomerReader`, `CustomerWriter`, and `CustomerReporter` when those capabilities have different consumers or implementations. A report controller receives only `CustomerReader`, while an administration use case can receive the write contract as well.

Adding an abstract method to a broad interface can force many implementers to change. Java default methods can preserve compatibility in some cases, but they do not make unrelated methods cohesive. The fix is a contract that accurately describes what each client needs.

question: How does ISP improve the flexibility of a codebase?
title: ISP and codebase flexibility — smaller interfaces, fewer forced changes
direct_answer: ISP improves flexibility by reducing accidental dependencies. When clients depend on focused capabilities, a change to invoice generation does not affect payment processors that never generate invoices. Implementations, tests, and consumers can change only where the relevant contract is used, provided the interfaces reflect real boundaries.

sections.title: ISP and Change Impact Reduction
sections.content:
Focused interfaces reduce the **change surface** of a capability. If refunds and invoices change independently, `Refundable` and `InvoiceGenerator` let clients depend on the one they use instead of a broad payment contract.

A new method still affects implementations of the interface that owns it, and consumers may need to adapt when the capability's meaning changes. ISP does not eliminate change; it keeps unrelated code outside that change.

The benefit depends on choosing real boundaries. Splitting every method into a separate interface can make construction, discovery, and navigation harder. Use consumer usage, implementation support, and change history to find the useful seams.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Small Contracts|~ISP effect|mix and match roles|implement exactly what's needed
blue|Looser Coupling|~fewer dependencies|a client sees only its methods
emerald|Easier Change|~localized|edit one role interface|other clients untouched
violet|Testability|~tiny mocks|stub one small interface

sections.title: Change Impact With and Without ISP
When Flexibility Matters Most
sections.content: ISP flexibility is critical in **plugin architectures** where different implementations provide different capabilities. For example, a document storage system with local file, AWS S3, and Google Drive backends — not all support versioning. ISP lets you add a Versionable interface without forcing local file storage to implement it. In **microservices with evolving APIs**, ISP allows one service to add features without breaking unrelated consumers. In **open source libraries**, ISP prevents breaking changes — you can add new interfaces without forcing every existing implementor to update. In **legacy system modernization**, ISP lets you incrementally refactor fat interfaces by extracting cohesive subsets, allowing gradual migration without a big-bang rewrite.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Promising that ISP removes all ripple effects**: implementations and clients of a changed capability still need review.
- **Using implementer count as the only metric**: examine which consumers use which operations and how the contract evolves.
- **Testing meaningless stub methods**: redesign the capability instead of normalizing invalid implementations.
- **Over-fragmenting**: too many tiny interfaces can make construction and navigation harder.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Focused interfaces keep unrelated consumers outside a capability change.
Clients can be tested with smaller fakes that model only the contract they use.
Implementations need to support only the capabilities they advertise.
ISP localizes change; it does not remove all change.
Split according to real usage and evolution, not an arbitrary method count.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
ISP improves flexibility by ensuring that a class depends only on the capability it uses. If invoice generation changes, payment implementations that never generate invoices should not be pulled into that change simply because both operations share one large interface.

For example, a card processor can implement `PaymentProcessor`, while only invoice-capable services implement `InvoiceGenerator`. An invoice controller depends on the second contract, and ordinary payment clients never see it. Tests also fake only the relevant methods.

This localizes changes rather than eliminating them. Implementations of a changed interface still need review, and badly fragmented interfaces add complexity. The useful boundary follows distinct consumers, supported capabilities, and change patterns.

question: How does ISP apply to Spring Boot application design?
title: ISP in Spring Boot — Repository interfaces and service interfaces
direct_answer: In Spring applications, apply ISP by giving each consumer the smallest useful contract. A read-only controller can depend on a query interface, while an administration use case can depend on a command interface. With Spring Data, choose or define repository interfaces deliberately; do not expose every persistence operation to code that only needs one query.

sections.title: ISP in Spring Boot Architecture
sections.content:
Spring does not apply ISP automatically. The principle appears when a component depends only on the operations it needs. A reporting controller may require `CustomerQueries`, while an administration service may also require `CustomerCommands`. The smaller contracts make permitted operations and test doubles easier to understand.

Spring Data offers repository interfaces with different capabilities, but their exact inheritance hierarchy depends on the Spring Data version and store module. `CrudRepository`, list-oriented CRUD interfaces, paging/sorting interfaces, and `JpaRepository` do not form a universal simple chain in every current version. Choose the supported contract for the application, or expose a narrower application-owned port in front of persistence.

A narrow Java type is not a security boundary by itself. Authorization must still be enforced at the request or service boundary. ISP improves dependency design; it does not replace access control.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Role Repositories|~Spring Data|narrow repository interfaces|expose only needed queries
blue|Service Interfaces|~per use case|NotificationSender, not GodService
emerald|Qualified Beans|~pick the role|fake in tests, real in prod
violet|Payoff|~clean wiring|small beans, easy mocks

sections.title: ISP in Spring Repositories and Services
When to Apply ISP in Spring Boot
sections.content:
Apply ISP when defining **service interfaces** that will be consumed by different types of clients. A REST controller that only reads data should depend on a read-only interface, not the full service.

Use ISP in **multi-layered security** — an admin controller can depend on UserAdminService, but a public API controller only gets PublicUserService with safe read methods.

Apply ISP in **testing** — if you are testing a component that only reads orders, mock OrderReader, not the full OrderService with 15 methods.

Use ISP when building **microservices** — an order service might expose OrderQueryService and OrderCommandService as separate interfaces, allowing downstream services to depend only on what they need.

Apply ISP when creating **Spring Data custom repositories** — if you need only two custom queries, do not force clients to see the entire JpaRepository surface.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Extending the largest repository by habit**: choose capabilities deliberately or hide persistence behind an application-owned port.
- **Assuming one Spring Data hierarchy for every version and store**: verify the current module's official API.
- **Treating a read-only Java type as authorization**: enforce access at the web or service boundary.
- **Injecting a narrow interface and later downcasting to the implementation**: that restores the dependency ISP was meant to remove.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Give each controller or service the smallest contract it actually uses.
Separate query and command interfaces when their consumers and change reasons differ.
Choose Spring Data repository capabilities deliberately; hierarchy details vary by module and version.
An application-owned repository port can hide a larger persistence API.
A narrow interface improves design but does not enforce authorization.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
In a Spring Boot application, ISP means that each class should depend on a focused contract rather than a large service or repository API. A reporting controller that only reads customers can depend on `CustomerQueries`; an administration use case that changes customers can depend on `CustomerCommands` as well.

The same idea applies to persistence. Spring Data provides interfaces with different capabilities, but their exact hierarchy varies across versions and store modules. I choose the smallest supported repository contract that fits, or place an application-owned interface in front of the Spring Data repository so business code sees only operations such as `findActiveCustomer` and `save`.

This reduces accidental dependencies and makes tests smaller because each consumer fakes only the methods it uses. It is not an authorization mechanism: a read-only type helps communicate intent, while Spring Security or service-level checks still decide who may perform an operation.

question: How is ISP different from SRP?
title: ISP vs SRP — interface segregation vs single responsibility
direct_answer: SRP asks whether a class or module has one primary reason to change. ISP asks whether a client depends on a contract containing operations it does not use. One concerns responsibility and change ownership; the other concerns the shape of client-facing capabilities. A large service and a fat interface often appear together, but either violation can exist alone.

sections.title: Distinguishing SRP and ISP
sections.content:
**SRP** evaluates responsibility: does this class or module serve one cohesive concern or actor, or do unrelated policies force it to change? **ISP** evaluates a client contract: does a consumer see only the capability it needs, or depend on unrelated methods?

A class can follow SRP but expose a fat interface. For example, one cohesive administration component may provide many operations, while a reporting client uses only one of them. Conversely, several narrow interfaces can all be implemented by one God Class that still violates SRP internally.

Fix SRP by separating independently changing responsibilities. Fix ISP by shaping contracts around consumer capabilities. Sometimes one refactor helps both, but the questions and evidence are different.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|SRP question|~Why does this unit change?|actor or policy|cohesive responsibility|implementation boundary
blue|ISP question|~What does this client need?|focused capability|no unused operations|dependency boundary
emerald|Can differ|~Independent problems|cohesive class + fat API|small APIs + God Class|diagnose separately
violet|Typical repair|~Match the issue|split responsibility for SRP|reshape contract for ISP|verify clients

rows: What clients are forced to implement
Class has multiple reasons to change
Interface has save and report methods

sections.title: When to Apply Each Principle
sections.content:
Apply **SRP** when designing or refactoring a class. Ask: does this class have one clear reason to exist? If a class handles user validation, sends emails, and logs to a database, it violates SRP — split it into UserValidator, EmailService, and AuditLogger.

Apply **ISP** when designing interfaces that will have multiple implementations with different capabilities. Ask: will all implementors actually use all the methods in this interface? If not, split it.

Use SRP during **code reviews** when you see a class file growing beyond 200-300 lines or when unit tests become hard to write because the class does too much.

Use ISP during **API design** when you notice some implementors stubbing out methods or when adding a new method forces unrelated classes to change. In practice, violations often co-occur, so fixing one helps the other.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling SRP the class version of ISP**: responsibility and client dependency are different questions.
- **Assuming small interfaces prove SRP**: one implementation can still own unrelated policies.
- **Assuming a cohesive class has a good client API**: a narrow client may still receive too many operations.
- **Applying both mechanically**: use actual change reasons and usage patterns.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: SRP concerns one primary reason to change for a class or module.
ISP concerns clients depending only on the operations they use.
A cohesive class can still expose a fat interface to a narrow client.
Small interfaces do not prevent one implementation from becoming a God Class.
Separate responsibilities for SRP; reshape client contracts for ISP.

sections.title: Code Example
Interview answer
sections.content:
SRP and ISP solve related but different problems. SRP asks whether a class or module owns one cohesive responsibility and has one primary reason to change. ISP asks whether a client-facing contract contains only the operations that consumer needs.

For example, a cohesive administration service may still expose a broad interface to a read-only report, which is an ISP problem. In the other direction, one large implementation can satisfy several small interfaces and still mix unrelated policies internally, which is an SRP problem.

The remedies follow the diagnosis: separate independently changing responsibilities for SRP, and provide capability-focused contracts for ISP. One refactor may improve both, but interface size and class responsibility are not the same measurement.
